name: Liam Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Liam. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you say stays confidential. Could you start by telling me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Right now I'm leading the joinery on a children's ward refurbishment at the district hospital, so a normal day starts with a briefing with the infection control nurse, believe it or not. Everything has to be sealed, dust sheets, negative pressure, the lot. Then it's fitting doors, skirting, nurses' station counters, and checking the work of the four carpenters under me. I've done hospitals and schools for about fifteen years now, it's fiddly work but it's steady.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy the finish. You hang a fire door so it closes on its own with a soft click, and nobody will ever notice it, and that's the point. The hard part is working around people who are sick, you're always aware you're in someone's worst week. And the hours, my wife Ana is a primary teacher and she's home by five, I'm often not.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any AI tools at the moment?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Now and then. My son Rafael, he's an electrician, showed me how to ask one about the fire door regulations, and it's handy for writing up a snag list neatly. I don't trust it on anything that matters, I always check the actual document. But I'll use it when it saves me half an hour at the kitchen table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it's a better search engine and a spell checker, no need to panic. At work I'd probably joke with the lads that the robots aren't coming for our mitre saws after all. I'm not really an online person, maybe a comment on the union's page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Personally, it means the next four or five years look like the last fifteen. I've got the savings, Ana's got her teacher's pension coming, and we paid off the house two years ago. I'd quite like that, honestly, a quiet finish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing, finish the ward and pick up the school job the firm's bidding on in the spring. I'd keep using the AI for the snag lists because it does save a bit of time. And I'd keep paying into the pension like normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pleasantly boring, I'd say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd miss out on, if AI stayed small?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a little. There's a part of me that hoped it would take the paperwork off foremen completely, the permits and the method statements. But I'd survive, I've filled those in by hand for thirty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Ana say about this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd be relieved for the kids at her school, she worries they're all going to be taught by a screen. She'd say good, let teachers teach. We'd probably talk about it over dinner for five minutes and then move on to the garden.

S0.say: It's a better search engine and spell checker, no need to panic. He'd joke with the crew that the robots aren't coming for their mitre saws.
S0.think: The next few years look like the last fifteen, with savings, a paid-off house and his wife's teacher's pension coming. He'd welcome a quiet finish.
S0.do: Keeps working, finishes the hospital ward and moves on to the school job in the spring. Keeps using AI for snag lists and pays into his pension as normal.
S0.quote: But I'd survive, I've filled those in by hand for thirty years.
S0.fieldNote: Liam is relaxed and practical, with a small hint of disappointment that AI wouldn't clear his paperwork. His sense of security is built on a paid-off house and two pensions. He brings his wife's view in naturally, which says something about how decisions get made at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is where the unions earn their money. If the work's changing, the training has to be paid for and the people who lose out need help across to the new jobs. At work I'd say, look, the old boys who won't touch a tablet need someone to sit with them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I think I'd be fine, maybe better than fine. Hospitals and schools are old buildings with weird corners, nothing's square, and somebody's still got to scribe a skirting board to a wonky wall. Where I'd worry is my daughter Inês, she draws plans for an architect, and that's exactly the kind of screen work that gets swallowed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get a bit more serious about the AI stuff, once I'd seen the other foremen using it properly. Maybe a two-day course if the firm paid, on the planning software. I'd sit down with Inês and talk through whether she should move toward site work or surveying, where you have to be there in person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, a bit of worry for Inês. I've seen a few changes come through this trade and we always adjusted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Inês, if she rang you worried?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her to come on site with me for a week. She's never seen a building go up from the inside, only on a screen. If she learns how things are actually put together, she's worth more than any program that only knows the drawing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you hold responsible, if people in your trade lost out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The firms, if they took the savings and didn't train anyone. And the government, for letting them. I don't blame the technology, a nail gun isn't evil either, but someone decides who gets the benefit.

S1.say: This is where the unions earn their money: training paid for and help across to new jobs. He'd tell work that the older carpenters who won't touch a tablet need someone to sit with them.
S1.think: His own work in old hospitals and schools is too irregular to automate soon, so he'd be fine. His worry is his daughter, whose drawing job at an architect's is exactly the screen work that gets swallowed.
S1.do: Takes AI tools more seriously once other foremen use them well, and does a firm-paid two-day course on planning software. Talks with his daughter about moving toward site work or surveying.
S1.feel: Mostly calm, with some worry for his daughter.
S1.quote: Somebody's still got to scribe a skirting board to a wonky wall.
S1.fieldNote: Liam's steadiness shows in waiting until other foremen prove the tools before he commits. He's confident about his own work and redirects concern to his daughter's drafting job. He separates the technology from the people who decide who benefits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next one is a lot faster. This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs stopping or slowing until there's a plan, and I'd say it at the union branch and I'd vote that way. You can't drop that on a hospital, on schools, with no rules. Online I'd be sharing whatever the union put out about a pause.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, at sixty I could walk away and we'd be all right, house is paid and we've got enough saved. But everything the kids built would be shaken, Inês's job, maybe Rafael's too if robots can pull cable. And I'd worry the pension fund takes a beating if the markets go mad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd sit down with Ana and our financial adviser and move some of the pension into something safer. I'd tell the firm I'll work as long as they need a human on these jobs, but I'd be ready to stop at sixty. And I'd set aside money for each of the kids, maybe ten thousand each, so they've got a floor if their work goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not for my own skin, for theirs. I'd feel like I'd done everything right and it might not count for much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd move ten thousand each to the kids. What would that cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The new van, probably, and the trip to see Ana's sister in Lisbon we've been planning. And maybe I'd work an extra year instead of two less. It's fine, it's what the money's for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the four carpenters under you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two of them are young, under thirty, and I'd tell them straight: get into the robot side, whatever that ends up being, maintenance or setup. The other two are near my age and I'd tell them to talk to the union about early retirement terms, now, before everybody's asking.

S2.say: This needs stopping or slowing until there's a plan, and he'd say so at the union branch and vote that way. He'd share union calls for a pause.
S2.think: At sixty he could stop and be fine, but his children's work would be shaken and his pension fund could take a beating. He feels he did everything right and it might not count.
S2.do: Meets his financial adviser in the first month to move pension money somewhere safer, and sets aside about ten thousand for each child. Tells the firm he'll stay while they need a human but is ready to stop at sixty.
S2.feel: Anxious for his children rather than himself.
S2.quote: I'd feel like I'd done everything right and it might not count for much.
S2.fieldNote: The fast scenario turns Liam's calm into worry about his children and his pension fund. He is ready to spend down savings to give the kids a floor, even giving up a planned family trip. His advice to his crew splits cleanly by age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Same end point, a bit more time. This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if we start now, so let's start now. At the branch I'd push for the union to get training deals in every contract. I'd probably say the same at the pub, where nobody would listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be sixty-three, so I'd have stopped. For me it's mostly the same worries as the fast one, but softer, because the kids have time to move. Inês could retrain, Rafael could get into installing the things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the thing the steady scenario made me think about, a proper course in the planning software, so I'm useful in the transition. I'd help Inês pay for a surveying qualification, part time. And I'd start trimming the risk in the pension a bit at a time instead of in a panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in control. Like seeing a storm on the forecast with enough time to bring the washing in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would five years change what you'd do on site day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. I'd make sure every young carpenter on my crew learns to hang a door by hand, because you never know when the machine's down. And I'd make sure they learn to work with the machine when it's up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You talked about Inês retraining. Has she ever wanted that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, she loves drawing. That's the hard part, telling your kid that the thing they're good at might not be wanted. I'd want her to make the choice herself, but I'd want her to make it early.

S3.say: Five years is enough to get ready if we start now. He'd push the union branch to get training deals into every contract.
S3.think: He'd be sixty-three and retired, with the same worries as the fast case but softer because his children have time to move into new work.
S3.do: Takes a proper planning software course to be useful in the transition and helps his daughter pay for a part-time surveying qualification. Trims risk in his pension gradually rather than in a panic.
S3.quote: That's the hard part, telling your kid that the thing they're good at might not be wanted.
S3.fieldNote: More time lets Liam act early instead of reacting, which suits his steady temperament. The emotional core is his daughter loving a job that might vanish. He wants hand skills kept alongside machine skills on his crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so no one gets to say they weren't warned. I'd tell the union that this is the time to win a shorter week and a share of the profits. I'd probably still be calm about saying it, I'm not a shouter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me personally, nothing. I'll be well retired by then, sixty-eight, probably doing woodwork in the shed and bothering Ana. The kids would have a decade, that's a lot, Rafael could be running his own business by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, retire around sixty-two or sixty-three like we'd planned, and hand over properly to the younger lads. I'd keep using the AI tools as they get better. And I'd talk to the kids every year or so about where things are heading, not lecture them, just keep it on the table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. I'd be a bit curious to see what a site looks like in 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you most like to see on that site?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like to see a robot carry plasterboard up four flights so nobody's back goes the way mine did. If that's what it does, good. I just don't want the bloke whose back it saved to be on the dole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change anything about your retirement date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I don't think so. Maybe I'd do a bit of part-time teaching at the college, show the apprentices the hand skills. That's something I'd do for pleasure, not money.

S4.say: Ten years is a gift, so no one can say they weren't warned. He'd tell the union this is the time to win a shorter week and a share of the profits.
S4.think: He'll be sixty-eight and retired, so it barely touches him. A decade gives his children plenty of time, and his son could be running his own business by then.
S4.do: Keeps his planned retirement at sixty-two or sixty-three and hands over properly to younger carpenters. Keeps using AI tools as they improve and checks in with his children every year about where things are heading.
S4.quote: I'd like to see a robot carry plasterboard up four flights so nobody's back goes the way mine did.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years Liam is calm and even curious, seeing robots as possible relief for workers' bodies. His fairness concern stays: the worker whose back is saved shouldn't lose their income. He floats part-time college teaching as something he'd enjoy.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because of the kids and because of the pension fund. What would help is if the government guaranteed pensions and put proper money behind retraining, and if the unions were at the table from day one, not after it's all been decided.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what we'd lose in hospitals. When I fit a nurses' station, I ask the nurses where they want the drawers, because they're the ones who'll use it twelve hours a day. I'm not sure a machine asks, and I'm not sure the firm would pay for the asking.

headlineQuote: When I fit a nurses' station, I ask the nurses where they want the drawers, because they're the ones who'll use it twelve hours a day.
portrait: Liam Santos is a 58-year-old lead joiner on hospital and school refurbishments, married to a primary teacher, with a paid-off house and two pensions in view. He uses AI now and then for snag lists and regulations but checks everything against the real document. He feels safe himself in every scenario and puts his worry into his children, especially his daughter, who draws plans for an architect. The two-year AGI picture makes him anxious enough to shift his pension and set aside money for each child. With more time he'd plan calmly, retrain a little, and keep pushing the union to share the gains.
biggestWorry: The 2028 scenario, because of what it would do to his children's work and to his pension fund.
whatWouldHelp: Government-guaranteed pensions, real money for retraining, and unions at the table from day one.
